## Why This Matters

In L20, PCA flattened four penguin measurements into a 2D picture and three species clouds jumped out —
but we *colored* them with species labels we already had. The common real situation has no labels: a
marketing table of customers with no segments marked, a pile of documents with no topics assigned, a set
of sensors with no "normal vs faulty" flag. **Clustering** finds the groups from the data alone.

This lesson runs the standard method, **k-means**, on the same penguins with the species hidden, and
watches it recover them — and then asks the two honest questions every clustering raises: *how many groups
are really there?* and *which points belong to no group well* (the outliers).

![Two side-by-side 2D scatter plots of penguins on the same principal-component axes. The left panel colors every point by the cluster k-means assigned with no labels; the right panel colors the same points by their true species. The two pictures match almost exactly: one tight group on the right (Gentoo) and two overlapping groups on the left (Adelie and Chinstrap).](assets/l21_clusters_vs_species.png)

**Reading the output:** handed only four numbers per bird and no labels, k-means recovers the species
**91.5%** of the time — the left picture (its clusters) and the right (the truth) are nearly the same. The
8.5% it misses are exactly the Adelie/Chinstrap penguins that overlapped in L20. Clustering is the
unsupervised mirror of L14's classifier: same goal of grouping, but learned without an answer key.

## Supervised vs Unsupervised

L14 built a **classifier**: it learned from *labeled* examples (penguins tagged with their species) and
predicted the label of new ones. Clustering is **unsupervised** — there are *no labels at all*. It groups
rows by similarity and leaves you to interpret what the groups mean. The two answer different questions:

| | L14 classifier (supervised) | Clustering (unsupervised) |
|---|---|---|
| Input | features **+ labels** | features only |
| Goal | predict the known label | discover unknown groups |
| Checked by | accuracy on held-out labels | judgment + (if you have labels) agreement |

We happen to *have* the species labels here, which lets us grade the clustering — a luxury you usually do
not get, and exactly why we hide them first.

## k-means

The most common clustering method is **k-means**, and the algorithm is short:

1. Pick **k** and drop k **centroids** at random.
2. **Assign** each point to its *nearest* centroid — a distance, exactly L18's vector norm.
3. **Move** each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it.
4. Repeat steps 2-3 until nothing moves.

What it is quietly minimizing is the **inertia** — the total squared distance from every point to its own
centroid (within-cluster spread). Smaller inertia means tighter groups. Two things to know up front: you
must choose **k yourself** (the method will not tell you how many groups exist), and k-means assumes the
clusters are roughly round and similar in size — it struggles with long, curved, or very uneven groups.

::: {.callout-note title="Standardize first (again)"}
k-means measures distance, so — like PCA in L20 — it is hijacked by the largest-unit column unless you
**standardize** first (L11's `StandardScaler`). Body mass in grams would otherwise dominate every
distance. Standardize, then cluster.
:::

## How Many Groups?

Since you must supply k, two tools help you choose it:

- **The elbow.** Plot inertia against k. It always falls as k grows (more centroids fit tighter), but the
  *rate* of improvement drops off at a "knee" — past it, extra clusters buy little. For the penguins the
  curve bends around **k = 3**.
- **The silhouette score.** A number from -1 to +1 measuring how well-separated the clusters are (each
  point compared to its own cluster vs the nearest other). Higher is cleaner.

![Two line charts. The left plots inertia against k from 1 to 6: it drops steeply from k=1 to k=3, then flattens, making an elbow around k=3. The right plots the silhouette score against k from 2 to 6: it is highest at k=2 (about 0.53) and declines steadily after, with a dashed line marking k=2.](assets/l21_choosing_k.png)

**Reading the output:** here the two guides **disagree** — the elbow suggests 3, but the silhouette is
highest at **k = 2**. Both are right about what they measure: k = 2 cleanly splits the big Gentoo from
everyone else (the single most obvious divide), while k = 3 matches the biology (Adelie and Chinstrap
overlap, so splitting them lowers the silhouette). The lesson: **k is a judgment, not an output.** The
metrics are guides; the right k depends on what you will *do* with the groups, and domain knowledge
(three species) breaks the tie here.

## Seeing the Clusters

Clustering pairs naturally with L20's projection: run k-means on the data, then **color the PCA scatter by
the cluster label** — using the 2D picture as the place to *see* groups an algorithm found. That is the
left panel of this lesson's opening figure. Comparing it to the true-species panel (a **crosstab** of
cluster vs species does the same numerically) is how you sanity-check a clustering when you are lucky
enough to have labels: 123 Gentoo land alone in one cluster, while the Adelie/Chinstrap overlap splits
imperfectly — the 91.5% story, made of real penguins.

## Outliers and Anomalies

The same distances that build the clusters also flag the **outliers**: a point's distance to *its own*
centroid says how typical it is. The points farthest from any center are the anomalies — the data an
analyst should always inspect before trusting a model.

```python
dist = np.linalg.norm(X - km.cluster_centers_[km.labels_], axis=1)   # L18 distance to own centroid
```

For the penguins the most extreme is a Gentoo from Biscoe at distance 2.88 — the same giant bird
(59.6 mm bill, 6050 g) L20's projection flagged in the corner. An outlier is not automatically an error;
it is a question: a real rare case, or a data-entry slip? Distance only tells you *where* to look.

## Another Way: Hierarchical Clustering

k-means needs k up front and starts over for each k. **Hierarchical** (agglomerative) clustering instead
builds a tree: start with every point its own cluster, repeatedly merge the two nearest, and record the
whole sequence as a **dendrogram**. You then *cut* the tree at whatever height gives the number of groups
you want — no k chosen in advance.

![A dendrogram: an upside-down tree where penguins merge into larger and larger groups from the bottom up, with the vertical axis showing the distance at which each merge happens. A dashed horizontal line cuts across near the top, slicing the tree into three branches.](assets/l21_dendrogram.png)

**Reading the output:** cutting this tree into three groups recovers the species **96.8%** of the time —
a different algorithm, the same biology, slightly cleaner here. Prefer hierarchical when you do not want to
commit to k in advance or when the *nested* structure matters (sub-groups within groups); prefer k-means
when the data is large (it is faster) and you have a k in mind.

## When to Use Which

- **k-means** — large data, roughly round groups, a k you can justify. Fast and simple.
- **Hierarchical** — you want to see structure at many granularities, or cannot pick k up front. The
  dendrogram is the payoff; it is slower on big data.
- **Just look at the PCA projection (L20)** — sometimes the groups are obvious by eye and you do not need
  an algorithm to assign them. Cluster when you need the *assignment* (which row in which group), not just
  the picture.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Clustering always returns clusters.** Even pure noise gets partitioned into k tidy groups. The
  algorithm never says "there are no groups here" — *you* must check that the clusters are real (separated,
  stable, interpretable), not an artifact of forcing k.
- **Forgetting to standardize.** Distances are unit-sensitive; the biggest-unit column dominates. Scale
  first, exactly as for PCA.
- **Treating k as an answer.** The elbow and silhouette are guides that often disagree; report the k you
  chose *and why*, not "the algorithm picked it."
- **Calling every outlier an error.** A far-from-centroid point is a flag to investigate, not a row to
  delete on sight.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Are the clusters real?"** — Clustering cannot tell you. Hand it random noise and it returns k neat
groups all the same. Validation is your job: do the clusters separate cleanly (silhouette), survive a
re-run or a resample, and *mean* something a domain expert recognizes? A cluster you cannot name is a
hypothesis, not a finding.

**"Is this the same as L14's classifier?"** — No, and the difference is the whole point. The classifier
needed labeled training data and predicts a *known* category. Clustering has no labels and proposes
*unknown* groups. They are sometimes combined — cluster first to discover segments, then train a classifier
to assign new rows — but they answer different questions.

**"How do I pick k?"** — There is no formula. Use the elbow and silhouette as guides, lean on domain
knowledge (we knew there were three species), and consider what the groups are *for*: a marketing team
that can run three campaigns wants k = 3 regardless of what the silhouette prefers. Report your reasoning.

## Cheat-sheet

| Task | Call |
|---|---|
| Standardize first | `StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)` |
| Cluster into k groups | `KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit(X)` |
| Within-cluster spread | `km.inertia_` (the elbow) |
| Cluster separation | `silhouette_score(X, km.labels_)` |
| Distance to own centroid (outliers) | `np.linalg.norm(X - km.cluster_centers_[km.labels_], axis=1)` |
| Compare to known labels | `pd.crosstab(km.labels_, true_labels)` |
| Hierarchical tree | `scipy.cluster.hierarchy.linkage(X, "ward")` + `dendrogram` |
